newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egyptian businessmen differ over deals with Israel.
newsitem.headline: Egyptian businessmen differ over deals with Israel.

text.p: Egyptian businessmen who met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and an accompanying business delegation on Wednesday are split on whether a warmer political climate is necessary for trade relations with Israel.
Netanyahu brought the business delegation with him on his second visit to Cairo in an attempt to kickstart economic relations that have been sluggish despite 18 years of peace.
Political relations between the two countries have cooled significantly since the right-wing Netanyahu took office as prime minister last June.
Most Egyptians are still wary of Israel and believe bilateral relations of any kind should wait until the Jewish state has made peace with its Arab neighbours.

Mohammed Hussein Geneidi, chairman of GMC Urban Environment Projects and a member of the Egyptian Industry Union, told reporters the one-hour meeting between Netanyahu and the business groups had brought the two sides closer.
"It was a very successful meeting. I think this meeting will be a turning point and will lead to greater economic and political closeness," Geneidi told reporters late on Wednesday.
Geneidi said Egyptian businessmen had accepted Netanyahu's invitation to visit Israel and the two sides had agreed to form an economic committee.
"We agreed that even if there are some political limitations, economic relations between us should not be frozen but that economic relations should push forward political relations," he added.
But Mohammed Farid Khamis, chairman of Oriental Weavers Group and head of the Egyptian Industry Union, was not so optimistic.

"True and complete peace in the region is a principal condition. Every step aimed at achieving peace will for sure be followed by more or equivalent steps aimed at developing economic relations in the Middle East," Khamis said.

"This means that Egyptian public opinion must be receptive to increased economic relations with Israel. Businessmen cannot work in a vacuum. The Israeli prime minister received this message very clearly," he added.
Khamis denied the two sides had formed a committee, as Geneidi said, and said that Egyptian businessmen would visit Israel when the political climate was right.

"They (Israelis) can give out all the invitations they want. Egyptian businessmen follow the Egyptian political line...If the atmosphere allows and they show us there is a true striving for peace, maybe we can think of a visit," Khamis added.
Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak has blamed Israel for poor bilateral economic relations, saying the Jewish state's policies towards its Arab neighbours have discouraged business people.

"I've already given the green light years ago for cooperation with Israel. It doesn't mean that I have to give the green light every now and then. I cannot press the people to go through, they are private sector," he told a news conference with Netanyahu on Wednesday.

"You cannot separate this from that because the people are affected by the political situation which may lower the key of much more cooperation. We intend to have good cooperation and the business people are allowed to work fully with your business people," he added.
Egyptian businessman Ibrahim Kamel broke the mould recently by buying a stake in Israel's Koor Industries as a political gesture to promote peace.
Kamel, chairman of the Kato group of companies, said the aim was to encourage the new Israeli government towards a settlement with the Palestinians.
